'''Albert Lee Toon Jr.''' (born April 30, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for eight seasons. A two-time First-team All-Big Ten pick at the University of Wisconsin, Toon set several school football records for the Wisconsin Badgers. The three-time [[Pro Bowl]] selectee played his entire NFL career with the Jets from 1985 to 1992, leading his team and the league in [[Reception (gridiron football)|receptions]] during the late 1980s. He is considered to be among the Jets' all-time greatest wide receivers and overall players in franchise history.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Schechter |first=Alan |date=February 26, 2016 |title=Five Best Wide Receivers in New York Jets' History |url=https://nflspinzone.com/2016/02/26/five-best-wide-receivers-new-york-jets-history/ |access-date=November 29, 2017 |website=NFL Spin Zone |publisher=Fansided |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201030341/https://nflspinzone.com/2016/02/26/five-best-wide-receivers-new-york-jets-history/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The 50 Greatest Jets|work=ESPN|publisher=ESPN Inc.|url=http://www.espn.com/newyork/photos/gallery/_/id/7157732/image/40/12-al-toon-wr-50-greatest-jets|access-date=November 29, 2017}}</ref>

==Early life==
In high school Toon was well known for his accomplishments in [[track and field]]. Toon is one of three [[AAA Peninsula District|Newport News Peninsula District]] athletes to surpass 50 feet in the [[triple jump]], which he did three times. He reached 23 feet in the [[long jump]]. Toon used that jumping ability as a wide receiver on [[Menchville High School]]'s football team.

Toon played [[College football|football]] and ran track at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] from 1981 to 1984.  Toon set a Big Ten single game receiver record while at the UW and established new school career football records for [[Reception (gridiron football)|receptions]] (131), receiving yards (2,103) and touchdown catches (19) at the end of this three season tenure for the Wisconsin Badgers. He also set Big Ten and school records in track and field in the Triple Jump while qualifying for the Olympic Trials in 1983 in the 110 High Hurdles and the Triple Jump.<ref>{{Cite web|title=2012 Fleer Retro - 1962 Fleer Design #62-AT|work=Fleer|publisher=UDC, Inc.|year=2012|url=https://www.comc.com/Cards/Football/2012/Fleer_Retro_-_1962_Fleer_Design/62-AT/Al_Toon/6465851|format=JPG|access-date=May 3, 2017}}</ref>

==Professional career==
He was selected by the [[New York Jets]] in the first round (10th overall) of the [[1985 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-09 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Toon made three catches for 67 yards in his first game against the Buffalo Bills in the 2nd week on September 15. He made a catch in eleven games, with his first touchdown being against the Indianapolis Colts on November 3 on a 17-yard catch from [[Ken O'Brien]]. His first big game came the following week with 156 yards on 10 catches against Miami, the most yards and receptions he had the whole season. In total, he caught 46 passes for 662 yards and three touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1986 Topps - #101 - Al Toon|work=Topps|publisher=Topps Chewing Gum, Inc.|year=1986|url=https://img.comc.com/i/Football/1986/Topps---Base/101/Al-Toon.jpg?id=13592ec9-c751-436f-ac61-f4dd918b6c6c&size=zoom&side=back|format=JPG|access-date=June 28, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=New York Jets at Indianapolis Colts - November 3rd, 1985 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198511030clt.htm |access-date=2024-01-15 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Toon 1985 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ToonAl00.htm |access-date=2024-01-15 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In the playoffs that season against the [[New England Patriots]], he caught nine passes for 93 yards in the 26–14 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild Card - New England Patriots at New York Jets - December 28th, 1985 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198512280nyj.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He had a breakout performance the following year, catching 85 passes for 1,176 yards with eight touchdowns. He was named an All-Pro and to the Pro Bowl while leading the team in receptions, which he would do for the next five seasons. In the Wild Card game that year, Toon caught four passes for 48 yards, which included a touchdown in the second quarter in the 35–15 victory (which ended up being the only postseason victory for Toon as a player). In the Divisional Round against the [[Cleveland Browns]], he caught five passes for 93 yards in the 23–20 loss in double overtime.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild Card - Kansas City Chiefs at New York Jets - December 28th, 1986 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198612280nyj.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round - New York Jets at Cleveland Browns - January 3rd, 1987 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198701030cle.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> His large stature in physicality and prowess as a blocker made him a suitable target on a variety of tough assignments for catches.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New York Jet Al Toon: Just Short Of Greatness |work=Jets Rewind |date=October 21, 2021 |url=https://jetsrewind.com/new-york-jet-al-toon-just-short-of-greatness/ |access-date=2024-01-16}}</ref>

The following season, he caught 67 passes for 976 yards for five touchdowns in twelve games. He was named to the Pro Bowl once again. The following [[1988 New York Jets season|1988 season]], he caught a league high 93 passes for 1,067 yards and five touchdowns while being named to the Pro Bowl and an All-Pro. He was the first Jet to lead the league in receptions since [[George Sauer Jr.|George Sauer]] in 1967; Toon is currently the last Jet to lead the league in receptions. He played in just eleven games in 1989, catching 63 passes for 693 yards with two touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Toon 1989 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ToonAl00.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He caught 57 passes for 757 yards in 1990 with six touchdowns under new head coach [[Bruce Coslet]], who called Toon a "consummate team player" while naming him team captain. 

He closed out his last full season in 1991 with 74 catches for 963 yards with no touchdowns. Toon made his last playoff appearance in the 1991 Wild Card game against the Houston Oilers. He caught a 10-yard touchdown pass from O'Brien to tie the game for the Jets in the second quarter, but the Jets lost 17–10. Toon caught eight passes for 96 yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild Card - New York Jets at Houston Oilers - December 29th, 1991 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199112290oti.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played in just nine games in 1992 and caught 31 passes for 311 yards and two touchdowns. Toon suffered a concussion against the [[Denver Broncos]] after a hit by [[Michael Brooks (defensive back)|Michael Brooks]] on November 8 during a reception that he caught, which went for eight yards while making it 101 straight games with at least one catch as a player. The hit knocked him unconscious and out of the game, which ended up being his last.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Toon 1992 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ToonAl00.htm |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

On November 28, 1992, Toon announced his retirement from the league, doing so after hearing from a handful of doctors that had each told him that he should not risk another blow to the head, as he had suffered five concussions in the last six seasons and nine in his career.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 27, 1992 |title=Toon retires after ninth concussion |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1992/11/27/Toon-retires-after-ninth-concussion/3710722840400/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Harvin |first=Al |date=1992-11-28 |title=FOOTBALL; With Sadness in His Eyes, Toon Bids Farewell |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/28/sports/football-with-sadness-in-his-eyes-toon-bids-farewell.html |access-date=2024-01-16 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He had set franchise records for receptions in a season (93) and consecutive games (110) at the time of his retirement. He was second in receptions (517) in team history to [[Don Maynard]] and third to Maynard and [[Wesley Walker]] in receiving yards (6,605).

Toon is one of two retired players in NFL history to play fewer than 110 games and still record over 500 receptions.  The other is Hall of Famer [[Kellen Winslow |Kellen Winslow Sr.]] Toon had more catches in his first five seasons (355) than any player in league history and reached 400 receptions in 81 games, which was third only to Winslow and [[Lionel Taylor]] (each 72) in history. In 2011, he was selected to the Jets Ring of Honor.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |last2= |first2= |date=2011-09-28 |title=Toon among four to be added to Jets Ring of Honor |url=https://nypost.com/2011/09/28/toon-among-four-to-be-added-to-jets-ring-of-honor/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==After football==
In 1995, Toon was one of nine founding members of Capitol Bank, a local community bank on whose board of directors he still serves. He was previously a president of the University of Wisconsin's National W Club, a varsity letter winners club. He also developed AT8 Companies to own, develop, and manage his commercial real estate portfolio. He also became both a Taco Bell franchisee and Hilton Garden Inn franchisee after his eight-year NFL stint. Additionally as a Community Center board member he and his team of locals developed the Boy's and Girl's Club of Dane County.
{{Quote box|quote=He probably should go down in history as one of the best wide receivers to ever play for the Jets. There weren't too many better than Al Toon playing anywhere in the NFL.<ref name="AlRamos">{{cite book|last=Prato|first=Greg|date=2011|title=Sack Exchange: The Definitive Oral History of the 1980s New York Jets|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_2hGA2U70hUC&q=%22al+toon%22+jets&pg=PA264|location=Toronto, Ontario, Canada|publisher=ECW Press|page=264|isbn=9781770410039}}</ref>
 |author = Frank Ramos, New York Jets  Director of Public Relations
 |source = ''Sack Exchange: The Definitive Oral History of the 1980s New York Jets''
 |quoted = 1
 |width = 33%
 |align  = left}}

Toon served on the [[board of directors]] of the [[National Guardian Life]] Insurance Company (NGL).<ref>[http://www.nglic.com/company/bod.jsp National Guardian Life Insurance Group - Board of Directors] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011020314/http://www.nglic.com/company/bod.jsp |date=October 11, 2007 }}, nglic.com; accessed July 26, 2017.</ref> He also served on the board of directors of the [[Green Bay Packers]]. Toon is now an owner of one of the largest privately owned and operated multifaceted design/build landscape companies in the Midwest, Olson Toon Landscaping, Inc.{{citation needed|date=July 2017}}
He is an investor in Wisconsin Burger King Franchise companies since 1992.
Toon, who suffered from [[post-concussion syndrome]], has improved to the point that he was able to compete in a triathlon in 2004.<ref>[http://www.ericmcerlain.com/offwingopinion/archives/003690.php Off Wing Opinion: A Comeback, Of Sorts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061124224441/http://www.ericmcerlain.com/offwingopinion/archives/003690.php |date=November 24, 2006 }}, ericmcerlain.com; accessed July 26, 2017.</ref>

==Personal life==
Toon is married to Jane and has a son and three daughters. His son, [[Nick Toon|Nick]], was a football standout in high school at [[Middleton, Wisconsin]] and played as a receiver for the Wisconsin Badgers, as his father did. His son passed him for all-time receptions and yards at the school in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Magliocchetti |first=Geoff |date=2019-08-14 |title=New York Jets Legend Al Toon Is Now Dominating Life [ESNY EXCLUSIVE] |url=https://elitesportsny.com/2019/08/14/new-york-jets-legend-al-toon-is-now-dominating-life-esny-exclusive/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Elite Sports NY |language=en-US}}</ref> Nicholas Toon was drafted by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the 4th round of the [[2012 NFL draft]] and played four years in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ToonNi00.htm|title=Nick Toon Stats|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>[http://wisconsin.scout.com/a.z?s=193&p=8&c=1&nid=2415550 Scout.com: Nick Toon Profile], wisconsin.scout.com; accessed July 26, 2017.</ref> He now owns and runs an online retail sales business along with a focus on real estate ownership and management with his wife.

His daughter, Kirby, attended UW–Madison as a preferred walk-on in volleyball.<ref name="kirby">{{cite web|url=http://www.uwbadgers.com/sports/w-volley/mtt/toon_kirby00.html|title=Player Bio: Kirby Toon|work=UWBadgers.com|access-date=November 19, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091113040500/http://www.uwbadgers.com/sports/w-volley/mtt/toon_kirby00.html|archive-date=November 13, 2009|url-status=live}}</ref> Kirby currently is working for Kimberly Clark. His other daughters, Molly and Sydney, also played volleyball. Molly was a [[NCAA Division I women's volleyball tournament|Final Four]] participant while playing volleyball at the [[University of Michigan]] and worked for Aerotek in Arizona, while Toon's youngest daughter, Sydney played two seasons of volleyball at University of Wisconsin Whitewater following her prep experience at [[Middleton High School (Middleton, Wisconsin)|Middleton High School]]. His daughter Molly was murdered in an apparent murder-suicide case by her husband in 2021.<ref>https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/molly-lillard-daughter-former-nfl-star-al-toon-dead-apparent-n1264197</ref>

'''Aldra Kauwa Wilson''' (born June 21, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for eight seasons with the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors.  Wilson was selected by the Denver Broncos in the first round of the [[1999 NFL draft]], and played his entire professional career for the Broncos.  He was a five-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection and a two-time [[All-Pro]] selection.

==Early life==
Wilson was born in [[Jackson, Tennessee|Jackson]], [[Tennessee]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rexrode |first=Joe |date=July 28, 2022 |title=Tennessee's recruitment of Al Wilson was a wild ride with long-lasting rewards |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3452288/2022/07/28/tennessee-recruiting-al-wilson/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811125110/https://theathletic.com/3452288/2022/07/28/tennessee-recruiting-al-wilson/ |archive-date=August 11, 2022 |access-date=February 25, 2023 |website=The Athletic |language=en}}</ref>  He was an [[All-America]]n performer at [[Jackson Central-Merry High School]] in Jackson,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shields |first=Brandon |date=January 30, 2017 |title=REMEMBER: Top signees of recent years |url=http://www.jacksonsun.com/story/sports/college/football/2017/01/30/remember-top-signees-recent-years/97246272/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225045433/https://www.jacksonsun.com/story/sports/college/football/2017/01/30/remember-top-signees-recent-years/97246272/ |archive-date=February 25, 2023 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=The Jackson Sun}}</ref> as named by BlueChip Illustrated, Max Emfinger, SuperPrep, and recruiting analyst [[Tom Lemming]]. In addition, he was named to the Tennessee all-state team.  Wilson was both a [[linebacker]] and [[running back]] at Jackson Central-Merry, rushing for 1,160 yards and 15 touchdowns in his senior season. He rushed for over 1,000 yards in three seasons in [[high school football|high school]], two as a running back and one as a [[quarterback]]. In addition to football, he starred in [[Track and field|track]] and [[basketball]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Wilson |url=http://tshf.net/halloffame/al-wilson/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731000234/http://tshf.net/halloffame/al-wilson/ |archive-date=July 31, 2017 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=[[Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame]]}}</ref>

==College career==
Wilson attended the [[University of Tennessee]], and played for coach [[Phillip Fulmer]]'s [[Tennessee Volunteers football]] team from 1995 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Wilson – Football |url=https://utsports.com/sports/football/roster/al-wilson/15634 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225045428/https://utsports.com/sports/football/roster/al-wilson/15634 ===Denver Broncos===

Over the course of his professional career, Wilson was the anchor of the Broncos' defense. Wilson made his NFL debut against the [[1999 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] in the Broncos' 1999 season opener.<ref name="1999gl" /> He recorded his first sack in Week 5 against the [[1999 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos at Oakland Raiders – October 10th, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199910100rai.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022134828/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199910100rai.htm |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=February 24, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He finished the 1999 season with 77 total tackles, four passes defended, and two forced fumbles.<ref name="1999gl">{{Cite web |title=Al Wilson 1999 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilsAl00/gamelog/1999 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170802182801/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilsAl00/gamelog/1999 |archive-date=August 2, 2017 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref> In his second season, he had five sacks, 61 total tackles, three interceptions, and eight passes defended in 15 games of the 2000 season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Al Wilson 2000 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilsAl00/gamelog/2000/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160622055118/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WilsAl00/gamelog/2000/ |archive-date=June 22, 2016 |access-date=February 25, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Free agency and retirement===
Wilson was cleared to return to resume playing by [[Los Angeles]] back specialist Bob Watkins in January 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=John |author-link=John Clayton (sportswriter) |date=January 10, 2008 |title=Ex-Broncos LB Wilson can return from neck woes |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3189580 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230225045433/https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3189580 |archive-date=February 25, 2023 |access-date=February 25, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> On February 12, he had his first visit of the offseason with the [[Detroit Lions]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zaroo |first=Phillip |date=February 12, 2008 |title=Report: LB Al Wilson to visit Lions |url=http://blog.mlive.com/highlightreel/2008/02/denver_post_lb_al_wilson_to_vi.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730225240/http://blog.mlive.com/highlightreel/2008/02/denver_post_lb_al_wilson_to_vi.html |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=[[Advance Publications]]}}</ref> He also visited the [[Cleveland Browns]] in March,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cleveland Browns checking out LB Al Wilson |url=http://watkinsspine.com/wp-content/uploads/pdfam/al_wilson_cleared_dr_bob_watkins.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160816145553/http://watkinsspine.com/wp-content/uploads/pdfam/al_wilson_cleared_dr_bob_watkins.pdf |archive-date=August 16, 2016 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=Watkins Spine}}</ref> but he rejected their offer for close to the veteran minimum.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

Wilson officially announced his retirement from professional football on September 10, 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=John |author-link=John Clayton (sportswriter) |date=September 10, 2008 |title=Former Broncos LB Wilson announces retirement |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3579956 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407002000/https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3579956 |archive-date=April 7, 2022 |access-date=February 24, 2023 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
After his career with the Denver Broncos ended, Wilson started a career as a Colorado football executive. Wilson became the co-owner of Project FANchise, which puts fans in control of professional teams. In addition, he acquired the [[Indoor Football League]]’s Colorado Crush.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jhabvala |first=Nikki |date=October 22, 2016 |title=Jhabvala: In new role with new team, Al Wilson is a part of Colorado football again |url=http://www.denverpost.com/2016/10/22/al-wilson-colorado-football-broncos/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730235832/http://www.denverpost.com/2016/10/22/al-wilson-colorado-football-broncos/ |archive-date=July 30, 2017 |access-date=July 30, 2017 |website=The Denver Post}}</ref>

'''Albert Lucas''' (September 1, 1978 – April 10, 2005) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]] (AFL). He died from a game-related [[spinal cord injury]] while playing for the [[Los Angeles Avengers]].

==Early life and college==
Lucas was born in [[Macon, Georgia]]; his father was [[Georgia State Representative]] [[David Lucas (American politician)|David Lucas]] and his mother was Macon City Councilwoman Elaine Lucas. He attended and played [[High school football|football]] for [[Northeast Health Science Magnet High School]].<ref name=obit>{{cite news|last=Ramati|first=Phillip|title=Son of Macon leaders killed in football accident|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/macon/obituary.aspx?n=al-lucas&pid=3402945|access-date=June 26, 2012|newspaper=[[Macon Telegraph]]|date=April 11, 2005}}</ref>  While there, he set the school record with a 440-pound (200-kg) [[bench press]]. Nicknamed "Big Luke", he went on to play [[college football]] at [[Troy State University]]. Lucas also served as an assistant football coach at Northeast High. He was married to De'Shonda Lucas with one daughter, Mariah.<ref name=usat>{{cite news|last=Haber|first=Bill|title=Former NFL player Lucas dies in Arena League game|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/football/2005-04-10-arena-lucas-death_x.htm|access-date=June 12, 2012|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=April 10, 2005}}</ref>  He was a member of the [[Omega Psi Phi]] fraternity.

At Troy State, Lucas was a standout player. In his senior year (1999), he won the [[Buck Buchanan Award]] as the most outstanding defensive player in [[NCAA Division I-AA]]. He was also honored with unanimous [[All America]] and All-Southland Football League first-team selections that year, in which he compiled 126 tackles (twenty for losses), 15 "quarterback hurries", four sacks, and two forced fumbles.

Lucas played a total of 43 games for the Trojans, and finished his college career with 255 tackles (thirty-six for losses), 25 quarterback hurries, and 11.5 sacks. In addition, he saw some limited action at running back in his junior and senior seasons, scoring seven touchdowns.

==Professional career==
After going undrafted in the [[2000 NFL draft]], Lucas signed with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the NFL on April 21, 2000.<ref name="pfa"/> He was later released on August 27, 2000.<ref name="pfa"/>

Lucas was signed to the practice squad of the NFL's [[Carolina Panthers]] on September 20, 2000.<ref name="pfa"/> He was promoted to the active roster on September 30, and played in 20 games for the Panthers over the course of the 2000 and 2001 seasons.<ref name="pfa"/> He totaled 49.5 tackles, three quarterback hurries, two batted down passes, a forced fumble, and a sack.<ref name=usat/> He was selected by the [[Frankfurt Galaxy (NFL Europe)|Frankfurt Galaxy]] with the fourth overall pick in the 2003 [[NFL Europa]] free-agent draft, but chose instead to begin his [[Arena Football League]] (AFL) career with the [[Tampa Bay Storm]].

In his rookie season with the Storm, Lucas had an immediate impact on his new team. He had 19.5 tackles, three for losses, 1.5 sacks, a blocked kick, and a safety, and was a major factor in the Storm's [[ArenaBowl]] victory over the [[Arizona Rattlers]]. He was named to the AFL's All-Rookie team,<ref name=heart/> and after that season, Lucas was one of the most sought-after free agents in the League, and signed a three-year contract with Los Angeles on October 27, 2003.

In the 2004 season, Lucas played in all 16 games for the AFL's [[Los Angeles Avengers]] and led the team's linemen with 18.5 tackles. He also had three quarterback sacks, three fumble recoveries (one for a touchdown), two batted down passes, a forced fumble, and a safety.<ref name=heart/>

==Death==
On April 10, 2005, in a game against the [[New York Dragons]], Lucas [[tackle (football move)|tackled]] [[Corey Johnson (American football)|Corey Johnson]] during a [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]] return with 10:17 to go in the first quarter. Replays showed that Johnson's knee hit Lucas' helmet, and Lucas did not move again after falling to the ground.<ref name=fbdies>{{cite news|last=Painter|first=Jill|title=Football player dies in game|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2005/04/11/football-player-dies-in-game/|access-date=June 26, 2012|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|date=April 11, 2005}}</ref> Later replays and reports showed nothing abnormal on the play.<ref name=norm>{{cite news|last=Maske|first=Mark|title=Arena Player's Death Followed A Seemingly Normal Collision|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A45119-2005Apr11.html|access-date=June 26, 2012|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=April 12, 2005}}</ref> Dr. William Lang, the team [[physician]], attempted to revive him on the field. He appeared to suffer a [[spinal cord injury]]. After being treated for approximately a half an hour at the [[Staples Center]], Lucas was rushed to nearby [[California Hospital Medical Center]], where he was pronounced dead at 1:28pm [[Pacific Standard Time Zone|PDT]].{{dead link|date=November 2021}}<ref name=afpd>{{cite news |last=Foster |first=Chris |title=Arena Football Player Dies After Injury |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2005-apr-11-sp-arena11-story.html |access-date=June 26, 2012 |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=April 11, 2005}}</ref> It is unknown whether Lucas died on the field, or after treatment failed. An autopsy revealed that he died of blunt force trauma and an upper spinal cord injury.<ref name=heart>{{cite news |last=White |first=Lonnie |title=Heartbroken |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-may-07-sp-lucas7-story.html |access-date=June 26, 2012 |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=May 7, 2006}}</ref>

Approximately half an hour after the game concluded, Lucas's death was confirmed by Avengers' primary team physician, Luga Podesta, who stated, "During the game today, Al Lucas suffered a presumed spinal cord injury and was brought to California Hospital Medical Center where all attempts to revive him were unsuccessful. He was pronounced dead at 1:28 p.m."<ref name=osc>{{cite news |last=Peterson |first=Tim |title=Avengers Win Overshadowed by Huge Loss |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/?id=3145457 |access-date=June 26, 2012 |newspaper=[[Our Sports Central]] |date=April 10, 2005}}</ref>

==Legacy==
The Avengers retired Lucas's number 76 during the 2006 season and the [[Tampa Bay Storm]] created the Mariah Lucas Scholarship Fund to benefit Lucas's daughter and wife, and the Lucas family itself started an Al Lucas Memorial Scholarship Fund which provides college scholarships to high school athletes.<ref name=heart/>

The [[Maxwell Football Club]] renamed its Arena Football League Player of the Year Award to the [[Al Lucas Award]] in honor of Lucas; this award was discontinued after the 2007 season.{{citation needed|date=June 2012}} The East Macon Park Little League field where Lucas played baseball was renamed Albert James Lucas "Big Luke" Memorial Field in 2006, and the AFL has renamed its Hero Award the Al Lucas Award.<ref name=heart/>

Harris played as a cornerback for 14 seasons in the NFL from 1998 to 2011. He played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]], [[Green Bay Packers]], [[Miami Dolphins]], and [[St. Louis Rams]]. He was selected for the [[Pro Bowl]] after his 2007 and 2008 seasons in Green Bay. The AP also named him a second team [[All-Pro]] in 2007. Harris was known throughout the league for his physical, [[bump and run coverage]] style and was also known for his long, stringy dreadlocks, influencing others in the NFL. He was drafted by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the sixth round of the [[1997 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas A&M–Kingsville Javelinas football|Texas A&M–Kingsville Javelinas]]. ==College career== Harris spent two seasons (1993–94) at [[Trinity Valley Community College]] in [[Athens, Texas]], where he was a member of the 1994 national championship team. He then transferred to [[Texas A&M University–Kingsville]] where he was a two-year starter and [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] (1995–96). Harris was a first-team All-[[Lone Star Conference]] pick in 1996. ==Professional career== ===Tampa Bay Buccaneers=== The [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] picked Harris in the sixth round (169th overall) of the [[1997 NFL draft]]. He was the 26th cornerback picked and was one of two cornerbacks selected by the Buccaneers in 1997, following third Round pick (97th overall) [[Ronde Barber]]. He was the 40th player selected from [[List of Texas A&M–Kingsville Javelinas in the NFL draft|Texas A&M–Kingsville]] since [[1967 NFL/AFL draft|1967]].{{Cite web |title=1997 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1997/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} On July 1, 1997, the [[1997 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] signed Harris to a rookie contract.{{cite web|title=Bucs sign three late round picks| url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1997/07/02/bucs-sign-three-late-round-picks/ |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=TampaBay.com| date=July 2, 1997}} He entered training camp as a backup and competed for a roster spot against [[Tyrone Legette]], Ronde Barber, and undrafted rookie Floyd Young. On August 24, 1997, the Buccaneers released Harris and placed him on waivers. On August 26, 1997, the Buccaneers assigned him to their practice squad after he cleared waivers. He remained on the practice squad throughout the entire [[1997 NFL season]].{{cite web| title=Al Harris Transaction History| url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/h/harr02500.html |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=profootballarchives.com}} He returned to training camp as a backup cornerback and was on the bubble, competing for the last roster spot as a cornerback against Ronde Barber and Floyd Young. The Buccaneers had retained starting cornerbacks [[Donnie Abraham]] and [[Anthony Parker (defensive back, born 1966)|Anthony Parker]] and also selected [[Brian Kelly (cornerback)|Brian Kelly]] in the second round of the [[1998 NFL draft]]. On August 30, 1998, the [[1998 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] released Harris as part of their final roster cuts. ===Philadelphia Eagles=== ====1998==== On August 31, 1998, the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] claimed Harris and acquired him after he cleared waivers. Head coach [[Ray Rhodes]] immediately named Harris the No. 2 starting cornerback for the upcoming season-opener in six days after [[Bobby Taylor (American football)|Bobby Taylor]] was placed on injured reserve after fracturing his [[scapula]] during their third preseason game against the [[1998 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]]. During the first quarter, Taylor made an interception and landed awkwardly on his shoulder as he fell to the turf and was expected to remain inactive for six–eight weeks.{{cite web| title=Eagles limping into regular season| url=https://www.poconorecord.com/story/sports/pro/1998/08/26/eagles-limping-into-regular-season/51100548007/ |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=PoconoRecord.com| date=August 26, 1998}} The Eagles only two backup cornerbacks were rookies [[Clarence Love]] and [[Allen Rossum]]. He would begin the season starting alongside [[Troy Vincent]]. On September 6, 1998, Harris made his professional regular season debut and earned his first career start in the [[1998 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles']] home opener against the [[1998 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] and recorded four solo tackles as they lost 36–0. In Week 3, he set a season-high with six solo tackles and two pass deflections during a 3–17 loss at the [[1998 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]].{{cite web| title=ESPN: Al Harris Game Logs (1998)| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/gamelog/_/id/1729/al-harris |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com}} He remained the No. 2 starting cornerback for the first five games before Bobby Taylor reclaimed his role after he had recovered from his injury. On December 28, 1998, the Philadelphia Eagles officially fired head coach Ray Rhodes after they finished the [[1998 NFL season]] with a disappointing 3–13 record. He finished the season with 41 combined tackles (40 solo) and seven pass deflections in 16 games and seven starts.{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Al Harris Career Overview| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HarrAl21.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} ====1999==== On January 11, 1999, the [[1999 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] hired [[1998 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] quarterbacks coach [[Andy Reid]] as their new head coach. The Packers coincidentally hired Ray Rhodes to be their new head coach on the same day. Throughout training camp, he competed against Bobby Taylor for the role as the No. 2 starting cornerback under new defensive coordinator [[Jim Johnson (American football)|Jim Johnson]]. He was named the starting nickelback and was listed as the No. 3 cornerback on the depth chart to begin the season, behind Troy Vincent and Bobby Taylor. On September 12, 1999, Harris started in the Eagles' home opener against the [[1999 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] and made five solo tackles, two pass deflections, and had his first career interception off a pass by [[Jake Plummer]] to wide receiver [[Frank Sanders (American football)|Frank Sanders]] during a 25–24 loss.{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at Philadelphia Eagles — September 12th, 1999| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199909120phi.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 5, he recorded one solo tackle and set a season-high with four pass deflections as the Eagles defeated the [[1999 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboy]] 10–13. On November 6, 1999, the Philadelphia Eagles signed Harris to a five—year contract extension. With one—year remaining on his previous contract, Harris was signed for the six—years throughout the [[2004 NFL season]].{{cite web |title = Al Harris Bio |url = http://www.packers.com/team/players/harris_al/ |accessdate = March 29, 2008 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20080319142135/http://www.packers.com/team/players/harris_al/ |archivedate = March 19, 2008 |url-status = dead }} In Week 10, Harris made two solo tackles, two pass deflections, and helped lead a fourth quarter comeback 28–35 victory against the [[1999 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] by intercepting a pass by [[Brad Johnson (American football)|Brad Johnson]] to wide receiver [[Albert Connell]] with less than five minutes left losing 28–27. Running back [[Eric Bieniemy]] would run for an 11–yard touchdown on the next drive to gain the lead 28–35 with 3:17 remaining. In Week 15, Harris made four combined tackles (two solo), had two pass breakups, and intercepted a pass thrown by [[Drew Bledsoe]] as the Eagles defeated the [[1999 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] 9–24.{{cite web| title=New England Patriots at Philadelphia Eagles — December 19th, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199912190phi.htm |access-date=June 24, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} On January 2, 2000, Harris made one solo tackle, a pass deflection, and secured a 31–38 victory against the [[1999 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] by intercepting a pass by [[Joe Germaine]] to running back [[Robert Holcombe]] and returning it 17–yards to score the first touchdown of his career with 1:20 remaining to increase their lead by 14 points to lead the Rams 24–38.{{cite web| title=St. Louis Rams at Philadelphia Eagles — January 2nd, 2000 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200001020phi.htm |access-date=June 24, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} This marked Harris's first career touchdown and his first pick-six, while also setting his career-high with four interceptions in a single season. He finished the [[1999 NFL season]] with 38 combined tackles (33 solo), 15 pass deflections, four interceptions, and one touchdown in 16 games and six starts.{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Al Harris Game Logs (1999)| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HarrAl21.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} He lined up as the nickelback throughout the season and had three starts at nickelback, with the other three as an injury replacement at outside cornerback. ====2000==== The [[2000 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] entered the [[2000 NFL season]] in their second season under head coach Andy Reid and second-year quarterback [[Donovan McNabb]]. Defensive coordinator Jim Johnson retained Troy Vincent, Bobby Taylor, and Al Harris at cornerback and [[Brian Dawkins]] at free safety, with [[Damon Moore]] replacing [[Tim Hauck]] at strong safety. In Week 15, Harris set a season-high with four solo tackles during a 35–24 victory at the [[2000 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]]. He finished the season with only 27 combined tackles (25 solo) and three pass deflections in 16 games and four starts. He was starting at nickelback throughout the entire season with Bobby Taylor and Troy Vincent starting all 16 games at outside corner. The Philadelphia Eagles went from a 5–11 record in 1999 to an 11–5 record in 2000, finishing in second in the [[NFC East]]. On December 31, 2000, Harris appeared in the first playoff game of his career and recorded two solo tackles and had one pass break-up as the Eagles routed the [[2000 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] at [[Veterans Stadium]] 3–21 in the NFC Wild-Card Game. They were eliminated from the playoffs the following week after losing 10–20 at the [[2000 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] in the Divisional Round.{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Al Harris Game Logs (2000)| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HarrAl21/gamelog/2000/ |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} ====2001==== He returned as the primary nickelback in 2001 and remained as the third cornerback on the depth chart behind [[Troy Vincent]] and [[Bobby Taylor (American football)|Bobby Taylor]]. On September 30, 2001, Harris recorded two solo tackles, three pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Anthony Wright (American football)|Anthony Wright]] to wide receiver [[Joey Galloway]] as the Eagles routed the [[2001 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] 18–40.{{cite web| title=Dallas Cowboys at Philadelphia Eagles — September 30th, 2001 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200109300phi.htm |access-date=June 24, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 12, he made two solo tackles, had one pass breakup, and secured a 23–10 victory at the [[2001 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] by intercepting a pass by [[Trent Green]] to wide receiver [[Larry Parker (American football)|Larry Parker]] with 3:09 remaining.{{cite web| title= Philadelphia Eagles at Kansas City Chiefs — November 29th, 2001 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200111290kan.htm |access-date=June 24, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} He finished the season with 22 combined tackles (20 solo), 12 pass deflections, and made two interceptions in 16 games and two starts. ====2002==== The [[2002 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] selected two cornerbacks in the [[2002 NFL draft]], including first round pick (26th overall) [[Lito Sheppard]] and second round pick (59th overall) [[Sheldon Brown (American football)|Sheldon Brown]]. Head coach [[Andy Reid]] retained Harris as the starting nickelback and third cornerback on the depth chart to begin the season, behind returning starters [[Troy Vincent]] and Bobby Taylor. On September 8, 2002, Harris started in the Eagles' season opener at the [[2002 Tennessee Titans season|Tennessee Titans]] in place of Troy Vincent, after he injured his knee during practice. Harris set a season-high with six solo tackles as they lost 24–27.{{cite web| title=Around the NFC| url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/2002/09/06/around-the-nfc/ |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=TampaBay.com| date=September 6, 2002}} On October 20, 2002, Harris set a season-high with three pass deflections and had his only interception of the season on a pass by [[Brad Johnson (American football)|Brad Johnson]] to wide receiver [[Keyshawn Johnson]] as the Eagles defeated the [[2002 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] 10—20.{{cite web| title=Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Philadelphia Eagles — October 20th, 2002| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200210200phi.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} He url=https://www.packers.com/news/packers-acquire-cb-al-harris-from-philadelphia-trade-wr-terry-glenn-to-d-2476476 |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Packers.com| date=February 27, 2003}}{{cite web| Coach Mike Sherman had been an assistant coach alongside Eagles' Vice President of Football Operations/Head Coach Andy Reid from 1997–1998 under [[Mike Holmgren]] for the [[1998 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]]. Entering training camp, it was expected that Harris would takeover as a starting cornerback following the departure of [[Tyrone Williams (cornerback)|Tyrone Williams]]. Defensive coordinator [[Ed Donatell]] began the season with Harris and [[Mike McKenzie (American football)|Mike McKenzie]]. {{quote box |align=right |width=50% |quote="He can come in and help us pretty quickly. I needed to fix the team right away with a player. He is very aggressive. He has good size and he challenges receivers."{{cite web| title=Eagles trade CB Al Harris to Packers |url=https://www.mrt.com/news/article/Eagles-Trade-CB-Al-Harris-to-Packers-7853855.php |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=mrt.com| date=February 27, 2003}} |source=–[[Mike Sherman]] [[2003 Green Bay Packers season|(Packers' GM/Head coach)]] }} On September 14, 2003, Harris made two solo tackles, one pass deflection, and had a pick-six by intercepting a pass by [[Joey Harrington]] to wide receiver [[Casey Fitzsimmons]] during a 6–31 victory against the [[2003 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]].{{cite web| title=Detroit Lions at Green Bay Packers — September 14th | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200309140gnb.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 5, he set a season-high with seven combined tackles (six solo) and had two pass break-ups as the Packers defeated the Seattle Seahawks 35–13. In Week 17, Harris made two solo tackles, two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Jarious Jackson]] to wide receiver [[Nate Jackson (American football)|Nate Jackson]] as the Packers routed the [[2003 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] 31–3.{{cite web| title=Denver Broncos at Green Bay Packers — December 28th, 2003| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200312280gnb.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} He started all 16 games for the first time in his career and made 48 combined tackles (46 solo), 14 pass deflections, and three interceptions. The [[2003 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] finished first in the [[NFC North]] with a 10–6 record in [[2003 NFL season|2003]]. On January 4, 2004, Harris started in the [[2003 NFC Wild Card playoff game (Seattle–Green Bay)|2003 NFC wildcard playoff game]] and made five solo tackles and one pass deflection in regulation as the Packers tied the [[2003 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] 27–27 to send the game into overtime. To start overtime, the Seahawks won a coin toss and received the ability to decide possession. Seahawks' quarterback [[Matt Hasselbeck]] said into the microphone to the crowd at [[Lambeau Field]] and to the national television audience, "We want the ball and we're going to score!" Both teams failed to score on their opening drives. On the Seahawks' second offensive drive, Harris would intercept a pass by Matt Hasselbeck to wide receiver [[Alex Bannister]] and returned it 52–yards for the game-winning touchdown to send the Packers into the Divisional Round. It was the first time a playoff game would have a defensive touchdown end overtime. On January 11, 2004, Harris would start in the NFC Divisional Round against his former team, the [[2003 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]]. At Veterans Stadium, he recorded four combined tackles (three solo) and had a pass deflection as the Packers lost 17–20 in their second consecutive overtime game. On the Packers' first offensive play in overtime, [[Brett Favre]] would throw a pass to wide receiver [[Javon Walker]] that was picked off by [[Brian Dawkins]] and returned 35–yards. This would lead to the game-winning field goal.{{cite web| title=Divisional Round — Green Bay Packers at Philadelphia Eagles — January 11th, 2004| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200401110phi.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} ====2004==== Defensive coordinator [[Ed Donatell]] was fired following the playoff loss to the Eagles. Head coach Mike Sherman promoted defensive backs coach [[Bob Slowik]] to defensive coordinator.{{cite web| title=Jan. 15, 2005: Sherman once again squanders chance |url=https://archive.jsonline.com/Services/include.ashx?domain=www.jsonline.com&file=186881612.html |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=jsonline.com| date=January 15, 2005}} The Packers used their first-round selection (25th overall) in the [[2004 NFL draft]] on cornerback [[Ahmad Carroll]] and used their third-round selection (70th overall) on cornerback [[Joey Thomas]]. It was speculated that the Packers' decision to use their top two picks on cornerbacks was related to an ongoing contract dispute with No. 2 starting cornerback Mike McKenzie.{{cite web| title=Packers pick cornerback Ahmad Carroll in the first round| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story?id=1789122&src=desktop |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=April 24, 2004}} McKenzie requested a trade or a contract extension and if neither of those demands were met, he'd continue to holdout and would even retire.{{cite web| title=Teammates would welcome McKenzie's return| url=https://www.packers.com/news/teammates-would-welcome-mckenzie-s-return-2473008 |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=June 4, 2004}} Harris entered training camp slated as the ''de facto'' No. 1 starting cornerback due to Mike McKenzie's training camp holdout. Head coach [[Mike Sherman]] named Harris and veteran [[Michael Hawthorne]] as the starting cornerbacks to begin the season. On September 12, 2004, the [[2004 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] signed Harris to a five—year, $18.70 million contract extension that included $7 million guaranteed.{{cite web| title=Packers addon to Harris's existing multi-year deal| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2764187 |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=February 13, 2007}}{{cite web| title=Al Harris signs contract extension| url=https://www.upi.com/Sports_News/2004/09/12/Al-Harris-signs-contract-extension/10421094998828/ |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=upi.com| date=September 12, 2004}} On October 4, 2004, the Packers officially traded [[Mike McKenzie (American football)|Mike McKenzie]] to the [[New Orleans Saints]]. On October 15, 2004, it was reported that Michael Hawthorne would be demoted and replaced by rookie Ahmad Carroll beginning in Week 6.{{cite web| title=LCB will replace veteran Hawthorne| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/columns/story?columnist=pasquarelli_len&id=1902836 |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=October 15, 2004| last=Pasquarelli| first=Len}} In Week 8, Harris recorded three solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and led the Packers to a victory at the [[2004 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] by intercepting a pass attempt thrown by [[Mark Brunell]] to wide receiver [[Rod Gardner]] as the Packers led 20–14 with 2:35 remaining in the fourth quarter. Harris returned his interception for 29–yards to the Washington 36–yard line and the Packers would cap off the drive with an 11–yard touchdown run by [[Ahman Green]] and successfully executed a two-point conversion for a 28–21 victory.{{cite web| title=Washington Redskins at Green Bay Packers — October 31st, 2004| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200410310was.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 12, Harris set a new season-high with eight combined tackles (seven solo) as the Packers defeated the [[2004 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] 45–17. He started all 16 games for the second consecutive season and set a career-high with 62 combined tackles (56 solo), set a career-high with 20 pass deflections, and had one interception. The Green Bay Packers finished the [[2004 NFL season]] a top the [[NFC North]] with a 10–6 record. On January 9, 2005, Harris started in the [[2004–05 NFL playoffs#NFC: Minnesota Vikings 31, Green Bay Packers 17|NFC Wild Card Game]] and recorded six combined tackles (five solo) to lose 31–17 to the [[2004 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]].{{cite web| title=Wild-Card Game — Green Bay Packers at Minnesota Vikings — January 9th, 2005| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200501090gnb.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} Harris was mainly responsible for covering star wide receiver [[Randy Moss]]. Late in the fourth quarter, Moss caught a 34–yard touchdown reception from [[Daunte Culpepper]] with Harris in coverage. Moss immediately ran next to the goal post, bent over, and pretended to "moon" the crowd at Lambeau Field. He states his motivation for his celebration was as a response to Packers fans throwing eggs at buses and actually dropping their pants and mooning buses of the visiting team as they arrive. The NFL would fine Moss $10,000 for the incident.{{cite web| title=Randy Moss rode big-play ability all the way to Hall of Fame| url=https://www.espn.com/blog/minnesota-vikings/post/_/id/26640/randy-moss-rode-big-play-ability-all-the-way-to-hall-of-fame |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=August 8, 2018}} ====2005==== On January 23, 2005, the [[2005 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] announced Mike Sherman's decision to hire [[Jim Bates (American football)|Jim Bates]] to be their defensive coordinator following the departure of Bob Slowik. This marked their third defensive coordinator in as many seasons.{{cite web| title=Packers name Jim Bates Defensive Coordinator| url=https://www.packers.com/news/packers-name-jim-bates-defensive-coordinator-2459387 |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Packers.com| date=January 23, 2005}} He returned as the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and was paired with Ahmad Carroll. On October 9, 2005, Harris made one solo tackle, set a season-high with three pass deflections, made one sack, and set a season-high with two interceptions off passes by [[Aaron Brooks (American football)|Aaron Brooks]], returning one for a 22–yard touchdown as the Packers routed the [[2005 New Orleans Saints season|New Orleans Saints]] 3–52. He had his first career sack on Aaron Brooks for a four–yard loss in the third quarter.{{cite web| title=New Orleans Saints at Green Bay Packers — October 9th, 2005| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200510090gnb.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 16, he had eight combined tackles (five solo) during a 17–24 loss against the [[2005 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]]. The following week, he made two solo tackles, one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass by [[Seneca Wallace]] to wide receiver [[Peter Warrick]] during a 23–17 win against the [[2005 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]]. He stated all 16 games for the third consecutive season and made 53 combined tackles (46 solo), 13 pass deflections, set a career-high with three sacks, made three interceptions, and returned one for a touchdown. He allowed only one touchdown in coverage. ====2006==== On January 2, 2006, the [[2006 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] fired head coach [[Mike Sherman]] following a 4–12 record in 2005. They hired [[2005 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers']] offensive coordinator [[Mike McCarthy]] as their new head coach. Entering training camp, Harris was slated as the No. 2 starting cornerback after the Packers signed [[Charles Woodson]]. Defensive coordinator [[Bob Sanders (American football coach)|Bob Sanders]] named Harris and Charles Woodson the starting cornerbacks to begin the season. [[File:Al Harris (Packers CB, 2006).jpg|thumb|left|Al Harris in 2006]] In Week 8, Harris recorded four solo tackles with four pass deflections as the Packers defeated the [[2006 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] 31–14. In Week 12, he tied his season-high of four solo tackles, made two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by Matt Hasselbeck to wide receiver [[Deion Branch]] during a 24–34 loss at the [[2006 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]].{{cite web| title=Green Bay Packers at Seattle Seahawks — November 27th, 2006| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200611270sea.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} In Week 15, Harris made two solo tackles, one pass deflection, and returned an interception thrown on a pass attempt by [[Jon Kitna]] to wide receiver [[Roy Williams (wide receiver)|Roy Williams]] for 34 yards during a 17–9 win against the [[2006 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]].{{cite web| title=Detroit Lions at Green Bay Packers — December 17th, 2006| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200612170gnb.htm |access-date=June 23, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}} He started all 16 games for the fourth consecutive season and made 41 combined tackles (35 solo), 13 pass deflections, three interceptions, and had one touchdown. ====2007==== On February 13, 2007, it was announced that Harris signed a two-year contract extension with the Packers. The deal was an add-on to the five-year, $18.7 million extension that Harris signed in 2004, a contract that included about $7 million in guarantees. That extension still had three seasons remaining on it, through 2009. Financial details of the new extension were not yet available, but Harris told the ''[[Wisconsin State Journal]]'' that it included two [[roster bonus]]es totaling $4.5 million, along with some [[Pro Bowl]] incentives.{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=February 13, 2007 |title=Packers add on to Harris' existing multiyear deal |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2764187 |access-date=December 10, 2023 |website=ESPN.com}} Harris played in the [[2008 Pro Bowl]], along with teammates [[Brett Favre]], [[Chad Clifton]], [[Donald Driver]], and [[Aaron Kampman]], as well as [[head coach]] [[Mike McCarthy]].{{cite web| url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3212177| title = Garcia, Schobel, Dockett, Cole, Albright added as injury replacements| date = January 24, 2008| work = ESPN.com}} ====2008==== Harris was originally thought to be out for the remainder of the 2008 season because of a ruptured spleen suffered during the first quarter of the game against Dallas, when he collided with fellow Green Bay Packer [[A. J. Hawk]]. However, Harris came back to the Packers in their game against the Tennessee Titans on November 2, 2008. ====2009==== On November 22, 2009, Al Harris suffered a potentially career-ending injury to the outside of his left knee in a home game against the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. Harris fell to the ground while trailing Niners wide receiver [[Michael Crabtree]]; no contact caused the injury, Harris reported his foot simply 'got caught in the ground'.{{cite web| url = http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/70766802.html| title = Packers 30, 49ers 24 - One up, two down| last1 = Silverstein| first1 = Tom}} Harris tore the [[anterior cruciate ligament]], the [[Fibular collateral ligament|lateral collateral ligament]], the [[iliotibial band]], the fibular collateral ligament, and the lateral hamstring. His knee was surgically reconstructed eight days later resulting in Harris spending the remainder of the season rehabilitating his knee.{{cite web| url = http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/95477594.html| title = Harris just wants to work| last1 = Nickel| first1 = Lori}} ====2010==== Harris started the 2010 season on the '[[Physically Unable to Perform|Physically Unable to Perform (PUP)]]' list, then returned to practice on October 19. On November 8, 2010, he was taken off the list and waived by the [[Green Bay Packers]].{{cite web| url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5779713| title = Packers corner Al Harris released| date = November 8, 2010| work = ESPN.com}} He passed through [[Waivers (American football)|waivers]] unclaimed, making him a [[Free agent (football)|free agent]]. Green Bay paid Harris the [[prorate]]d portion of his $2.5 million salary, as the team was not obligated to pay the rest even though he passed through waivers.{{Cite web |url= http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Friday-new-and-note-1727.html |title= Friday new$ and note$ {{!}} National Football Post |access-date=November 15, 2010 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20101115211311/http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Friday-new-and-note-1727.html |archive-date= November 15, 2010 |url-status=dead }} On Sunday, November 21, 2010, Harris took out a large advertisement in the ''[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]]'', thanking Packer fans for 'always supporting (him)'.{{cite web| url = http://www.jsonline.com/news/109859129.html| title = Al Harris' thank you note}} The Packers won the [[Super Bowl XLV|Super Bowl]] that year, and Harris received a championship ring.{{Cite web |url=http://blogs.greenbaypressgazette.com/blogs/gpg/insider/2011/05/12/murphy-al-harris-to-get-super-bowl-ring |title=Packersnews.com {{!}} Green Bay Packers {{!}} Insiders Blog» Murphy: Al Harris to get Super Bowl ring |access-date= May 15, 2011 }}{{dead link|date=November 2018|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} ===Miami Dolphins=== Harris signed a 1-year deal with the [[Miami Dolphins]] on November 10, 2010.{{cite web| url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5787349| title = Al Harris signs with Dolphins| date = November 10, 2010}} He played three games before suffering a hamstring injury and was placed on injured reserve. On December 30, 2010, the Dolphins reached an injury settlement with Harris and he was released.{{cite web| url = http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Source-Al-Harris-cut-from-injured-reserve.html| title = Al Harris cut from Injured Reserve| access-date = September 17, 2011| archive-date = April 2, 2012| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120402004005/http://www.nationalfootballpost.com/Source-Al-Harris-cut-from-injured-reserve.html| url-status = dead}} ===St. Louis Rams=== On July 29, 2011, Harris agreed to terms with the [[St. Louis Rams]]. On November 13, 2011, Harris suffered a torn [[anterior cruciate ligament|ACL]] in his right knee during a regular season game against the [[Cleveland Browns]] and did not return to the game. The following day, November 14, 2011, Harris was placed on injured reserve. ===Retirement=== On May 1, 2013, [[Ted Thompson]], Packers Executive Vice President, General Manager and Director of Football Operations, stated that Al Harris had informed the team of his decision to retire as a Green Bay Packer.{{Cite web |url=http://www.channel3000.com/sports/packers/al-harris-to-retire-as-a-packer/-/4058/19976552/-/c79j71z/-/index.html |title=Al Harris to retire as a Packer | Packers - Channel3000.com |access-date=May 2, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130503101332/http://www.channel3000.com/sports/packers/al-harris-to-retire-as-a-packer/-/4058/19976552/-/c79j71z/-/index.html |archive-date=May 3, 2013 |url-status=dead }} When asked to comment Harris said, "Just over my career I had an awesome time, but the better part of my years were in Green Bay, (so) it was just important to me to retire as a Packer," nearly three-and-a-half years since he played his final snap for the Packers. "I had a great experience in Philadelphia, great experience in Tampa and everywhere else I played, but Green Bay is a special place to play football."{{cite web| url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/9236894/cornerback-al-harris-retires-green-bay-packers| title = CB Al Harris retires as a Packer| date = May 2, 2013| work=ESPN.com}} In 2021, Harris was inducted into the [[Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame]].{{Cite web | url = https://www.packers.com/history/hof/al-harris | title = Al Harris | last = Christl | first = Cliff | author-link = Cliff Christl | website = Packers.com | access-date = September 20, 2023 | archive-date = May 29, 2023 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230529221620/https://www.packers.com/history/hof/al-harris | url-status = live }} ==Coaching career== ===Miami Dolphins=== During the [[2012 NFL season|2012]] season, Harris served as a coaching intern under coach [[Joe Philbin]] for the Miami Dolphins.{{cite web| url = http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2012-07-27/sports/sfl-miami-dolphins-training-camp-072712_1_joe-philbin-david-garrard-ryan-tannehill/2| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140903120807/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2012-07-27/sports/sfl-miami-dolphins-training-camp-072712_1_joe-philbin-david-garrard-ryan-tannehill/2| url-status = dead| archive-date = September 3, 2014| title = Miami Dolphins training camp report - Day 1 - Page 2 - Sun Sentinel}} ===Kansas City Chiefs=== Harris was hired as the assistant defensive backs coach for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] under his former head coach from his playing day with the [[Philadelphia Eagles|Eagles]], [[Andy Reid]], on January 25, 2013.{{cite news|title=Al Harris to coach Chiefs secondary|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8881997/al-harris-former-defensive-back-joins-kansas-city-chiefs-staff|agency=Associated Press|access-date=January 26, 2013}} Following a disappointing performance by the Chiefs defense in the [[2018–19 NFL playoffs#AFC: New England Patriots 37, Kansas City Chiefs 31 (OT)|AFC Championship game]] for the [[2018 Kansas City Chiefs season|2018 season]], the entire defensive coaching staff, including Harris, was replaced.{{cite web |title=Chiefs Finalize Defensive Coaching Staff |url=https://www.chiefs.com/news/chiefs-finalize-defensive-coaching-staff?sf208036019=1 |website=Chiefs.com}} ===Dallas Cowboys=== In [[2020 NFL season|2020]], Harris was hired to work as the [[Dallas Cowboys]]' secondary coach, reuniting him with former Packers coach and new Cowboys head coach [[Mike McCarthy]].{{Cite web|url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2020/01/16/cowboys-hire-al-harris-to-work-with-secondary/|title=Cowboys hire Al Harris to work with secondary|last=Williams|first=Charean|date=2020-01-17|website=ProFootballTalk|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-20}} Under Harris' coaching in 2021, sophomore cornerback [[Trevon Diggs]] tied a franchise record 11 interceptions on the year, and he was named to the Pro Bowl and First-Team All Pro. In 2023, another sophomore cornerback, [[DaRon Bland]], set the NFL record for most pick-sixes in a single season with 5, and he too was named a Pro Bowler and First-Team All Pro as he led the league in interceptions.{{Cite web |last=Silverman |first=Steve |date=2023-11-24 |title=Lakers' LeBron James honors DaRon Bland after historic pick-6 |url=https://clutchpoints.com/cowboys-news-lakers-lebron-james-gives-daron-bland-his-flowers-after-historic-pick-6 |access-date=2024-06-23 |website=ClutchPoints |language=en}} ===Chicago Bears=== In January 2025, Harris was hired by the [[Chicago Bears]] as their defensive backs coach and defensive passing game coordinator under new head coach [[Ben Johnson (American football coach)|Ben Johnson]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.dallascowboys.com/news/al-harris-headlines-recent-round-of-coaching-departures-from-cowboys |title=Al Harris headlines recent round of coaching departures from Cowboys }} He had previously coached alongside Johnson on the Dolphins' staff in 2012. The 2025 Bears defense led the league in interceptions with 23.{{cite magazine|last=Coley|first=Joanne|url=https://www.si.com/nfl/commanders/onsi/news/washington-commanders-defensive-coordinator-search-al-harris-brian-flores-dan-quinn-reunion|title=Al Harris Emerges as a Serious Candidate for Commanders Defensive Coordinator|magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]]|date=January 24, 2026|access-date=February 10, 2026}} Safety [[Kevin Byard]] had a league-high seven interceptions while cornerback [[Nahshon Wright]] topped all NFL cornerbacks with five picks, earning both of them Pro Bowl selections. Wright, who was considered a fringe player before joining the Bears in 2025, credited Harris at the Pro Bowl as "the reason why I'm standing here today."{{cite news|last=Noble|first=Kole|url=https://atozsports.com/nfl/chicago-bears-news/bears-ben-johnson-scores-one-big-win-al-harris-nahshon-wright-free-agency/|title=Ben Johnson officially scores one big win with the coaching staff and it could help retain a top free agent|publisher=A to Z Sports|date=February 3, 2026|access-date=February 10, 2026}} Johnson also praised Harris for doing a "phenomenal phenomenal job" throughout the season.{{cite news|last=Noble|first=Kole|url=https://atozsports.com/nfl/chicago-bears-news/bears-cj-gardner-johnson-introduction-al-harris-antwaan-randle-el-week-17/|title=Bears defensive back just made two assistant coaches smile without even doing anything on the field and it came at the most fitting time|publisher=A to Z Sports|date=December 28, 2025|access-date=February 10, 2026}} ==NFL statistics== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |- ! June 16, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player and actor. He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]] before being selected fifth overall in the first round by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the [[1970 NFL draft]]. He was a [[starting lineup|starter]] at various defensive positions for the [[Buffalo Bills]], [[Houston Oilers]], [[Los Angeles Rams]], [[Seattle Seahawks]], and the [[San Francisco 49ers]], until retiring after the 1979 season.{{cite magazine |last1=Swift |first1=E.M. |date=1994-06-27 |title=Friends To The End |url=https://www.si.com/vault/issue/711111 |access-date=2019-06-16 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |page=46 |volume=80 |issue=25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802182816/https://www.si.com/vault/issue/711111 |archive-date=August 2, 2019 }}Marcin (1971), p. 56.
Ebony (Nov 1974), p. 170.
Ebony (Nov 1977), pp. 170–172. Cowlings is most famous for his role in aiding his close friend [[O. J. Simpson]] in [[White Bronco chase|fleeing the police]] on June 17, 1994, after Simpson was [[Murder trial of O. J. Simpson|accused of killing]] his ex-wife [[Nicole Brown Simpson]] and her friend [[Ron Goldman]]. After leading police on a low-speed chase in his now infamous white [[Ford Bronco]] (not to be confused with Simpson's own Ford Bronco, which had traces of the victims' blood and was therefore used as evidence in the trial), Cowlings drove Simpson back to his home where both were arrested; Simpson for murder, and Cowlings for aiding a fugitive, although the charges against Cowlings would later be dropped. ==Early life== Cowlings was born on June 16, 1947, in San Francisco, and raised in its [[Potrero Hill, San Francisco|Potrero Hill]] neighborhood. There he was a member of the Superiors social club, which met at the Booker T. Washington Community Center. He attended [[Galileo Academy of Science and Technology|Galileo High School]], where he played football with [[O. J. Simpson]]. He and Simpson became friends.de Lama, George (June 21, 1994) [https://www.chicagotribune.com/1994/06/21/cowlings-simpson-inseparable-even-as-teens/ "Cowlings, Simpson Inseparable, Even As Teens."] ''Chicago Tribune.'' (Retrieved January 7, 2014.)Wolf, Craig (June 19, 1994) [https://www.nytimes.com/1994/06/19/nyregion/the-simpson-case-the-friend-a-lifelong-loyalty-true-to-the-end.html "The Simpson Case: The Friend; A Lifelong Loyalty, True to the End."] ''New York Times.'' (Retrieved January 7, 2014.) After high school, both attended [[City College of San Francisco]], where they played on the football team. ==Football career== Cowlings was named an [[All-American]] [[defensive tackle]] after his senior year at the [[University of Southern California]] (USC).{{Cite web|url=http://beckys-place.com/cowlings.html|title = Seattle Seahawks Spirit of 1976 Page}} During his senior year, the Trojans went undefeated, and Cowlings led a powerful defensive line, nicknamed "The Wild Bunch" after [[The Wild Bunch|the movie of the same name]]. Cowlings was drafted fifth in the first round of the [[1970 NFL draft]] by the [[Buffalo Bills]]. He was a starter his first three years in Buffalo, but was traded to [[Houston Oilers]] after the 1972 season. He played all 14 games for the Oilers in both 1973 and 1974, but just five games in 1975 for the [[Los Angeles Rams|Rams]]. In 1976, he became a charter member of the [[Seattle Seahawks]], after being signed off the [[Waivers (American football)|waiver wire]] when the Rams released him at the end of the preseason. He played just one game, due to an injury he suffered while playing for the Rams in an exhibition game against the Seahawks. He returned to the Rams in 1977, played with CFL [[Montreal Alouettes]] in 1978, and finished his career in 1979 with the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. ==Acting career== Cowlings's first film role was in the 1985 film ''Bubba Until It Hurts'', starring [[Bubba Smith]]. He had a recurring minor role as Coach Nabors in the [[HBO]] football sitcom ''[[1st & Ten (1984 TV series)|1st & Ten]]'', which also starred Simpson. Cowlings also served as a technical football advisor on the football scenes in the 1991 [[Tony Scott]] film ''[[The Last Boy Scout]]''. ==Friendship with O. J. Simpson== [[File:O.J. Simpson 1990 · DN-ST-91-03444 crop.JPEG|thumb|Cowlings was a close friend of [[O. J. Simpson]], whom he had known since childhood]] Cowlings was a close friend of [[O. J. Simpson]], whom he had known since childhood. They were teammates at [[Galileo High School]], [[San Francisco City College]], [[University of Southern California|USC]], on the Buffalo Bills, and on the San Francisco 49ers. Cowlings dated Simpson's first wife, Marguerite Whitley, while they were attending Galileo High School, and when they were having issues as a couple, Simpson stepped in as a mediator, but the discussion turned into a relationship and they married in 1967; Cowlings was reportedly angry at the time, but he and Simpson would eventually reconcile and resume their friendship.{{Cite web |url=https://www.ksat.com/inside-edition/oj-simpsons-forgotten-first-wife-who-is-marguerite-whitley |title=O.J. Simpson's Forgotten First Wife: Who is Marguerite Whitley? |access-date=May 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802182820/https://www.ksat.com/inside-edition/oj-simpsons-forgotten-first-wife-who-is-marguerite-whitley |archive-date=August 2, 2019 |url-status=dead }} They remained close friends and confidants through the years, with Cowlings being the godfather of Simpson's son Jason and a [[groomsman]] at Simpson's and [[Nicole Brown Simpson|Nicole Brown]]'s wedding in 1985. Cowlings was also the [[ring bearer]] at mutual friends [[Robert Kardashian|Robert]] and [[Kris Jenner|Kris Kardashian]]'s wedding in 1978.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oNiJcJE1GkYC&q=al+cowlings+groomsman&pg=PA51|title = Kris Jenner . . . And All Things Kardashian|isbn = 9781451646979|last1 = Jenner|first1 = Kris|date = September 4, 2012| publisher=Simon and Schuster }} ===Bronco chase=== {{Main|Bronco chase}} [[File:FORD-Bronco.jpg|left|thumb|300x300px|A [[Ford Bronco#Fifth generation (1992-1996)|fifth-generation Ford Bronco]] similar to the model driven by Cowlings]] After the murders of Nicole Brown and her friend [[Ronald Goldman]] on June 12, 1994, in which Simpson was a "person of interest," Brown's funeral took place in the [[St. Martin of Tours Catholic Church]] in Brentwood on June 16, Cowlings's 47th birthday; Cowlings served as a [[gatekeeper]] and [[pallbearer]] at the funeral. During the memorial service at David LeBon's house, Cowlings paid his respects to Brown while holding back tears.{{OSM Location map||float=right|coord={{Coord|33.81|-117.98}}|zoom=9|width=500|height=300|scalemark=20|mark-size1=18|caption=Selected key locations of the Bronco chase{{cite video |title=[[30 for 30]]: June 17, 1994 |medium=television |people=Brett Morgen, director |date=June 16, 2010 |publisher=ESPN}}{{cite web|url=https://la.curbed.com/maps/oj-simpson-map-murder-sites-los-angeles-brentwood-bronco-chase|title=The OJ Simpson White Ford Bronco Chase Map of Los Angeles|first=Adrian Glick|last=Kudler|work=[[Curbed]]|publisher=[[Vox Media]]|date=February 2, 2016|access-date=April 3, 2021|archive-date=November 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201110112433/https://la.curbed.com/maps/oj-simpson-map-murder-sites-los-angeles-brentwood-bronco-chase|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/oj-simpson-white-bronco-chase-map-photo-204447645.html|title='The People v. Later that day, witnesses reported seeing Simpson riding in a white [[Ford Bronco]], a vehicle owned and being driven by Cowlings, thus becoming the object of a low-speed chase by [[California Highway Patrol]] cruisers on the freeways. During the chase, Cowlings made a 911 call from a cell phone and claimed that Simpson was armed with a gun pointed at his own head, demanding that Cowlings drive him to Simpson's estate in [[Brentwood, Los Angeles, California|Brentwood]], or Simpson would kill himself. The pursuit was televised on live TV via helicopter, interrupted coverage of the [[1994 NBA Finals]], and was viewed by approximately 95 million people in the United States alone. During the chase, an agitated Cowlings famously told 911 dispatchers: "My name is A.C.! You know who I am, goddamn it!" The chase ended at Simpson's Brentwood home, where Simpson surrendered to police after a nearly hour-long wait.Bugliosi (1997), p. 126. When the chase concluded and Cowlings and Simpson surrendered, Cowlings was arrested and charged with a [[felony]] for aiding a fugitive. He was booked into the Los Angeles men's jail, from which he was later released on a $250,000 bond.{{cite news |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8LoDAAAAMBAJ&q=simpson+o+j+white+bronco&pg=PA4 |title=O.J. Simpson's Bizarre Saga In Ex-Wife's Murder Ends In Not Guilty Plea |access-date=March 26, 2011 |date=July 4, 1994 |publisher=Jet |pages=4}} District Attorney [[Gil Garcetti]] eventually determined, however, that pending charges against Cowlings would be dropped due to a lack of sufficient evidence. In 1994, Cowlings's 1993 Ford Bronco from the low-speed chase was purchased by Simpson's former sports agent [[Mike Gilbert]] and two other men, then ended up sitting in a parking garage for the next 17 years (1995–2012), where it was rarely used.{{cite news |last1=Breech |first1=John |date=2019-06-17 |title=Here's what happened to the white Ford Bronco from the O.J.
